extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and theatre practitioners interested in Shakespeare's Twelfth Night
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative considerations for producing, adapting, or interpreting Shakespeare's Twelfth Night (performance, film, musical, or other media), focusing on choices that affect tone, casting, music, setting, and thematic emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve the carnival-like/carnivalesque atmosphere
rubrics_metrics.description: The history of festive ritual and carnivalesque reversal is the cultural origin of the play's gender-confusion-driven plot; the play has been regarded as preserving this festive and traditional atmosphere of licensed disorder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Productions should consider emphasising the inversion of order, revelry and licensed disorder (masters as servants, role-reversal) to sustain the play's comic energy. Example: productions that foreground convivial, carnivalesque tone (e.g., Liviu Ciulei's 1984 ‘circus world’) highlight this origin. Anti-pattern: staging that strips away the sense of licensed revelry may weaken the play's thematic core.

rubrics_metrics.name: Casting and gender-presentation choices
rubrics_metrics.description: When the play was first performed, all female parts were played by men or boys; modern practice varies from casting women in female parts to intentional all-male or gender-swapped casting (e.g., Propeller's all-male productions, 2017 National Theatre’s change of Malvolio to Malvolia).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to use historical casting (all-male), conventional modern casting (women for female parts), or gender-swapped/innovative casting to foreground or interrogate gender identity and sexuality. Examples: all-male casts emphasise theatrical gender play; gender-swaps (Malvolia) can change readings of sexuality and power. Consider how casting affects audience perception of androgyny, sexual ambiguity, and gender transgression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of the Malvolio subplot and its tone
rubrics_metrics.description: The embittered and isolated Malvolio can be regarded as an adversary of festive enjoyment and community; productions and critics often focus on how his humiliation is handled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether Malvolio’s plot is played for broad comedy, sympathy, or darker cruelty. Many actors and productions emphasize Malvolio (he is a 'popular character choice'); adaptations and revivals vary in how they resolve his humiliation (from comic payoff to problematic cruelty). Anti-pattern: treating the subplot carelessly can leave the ending tonally unresolved or alienate audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of comedy versus dramatic seriousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Some adaptations downplay comic material into straightforward drama (e.g., Trevor Nunn's 1996 film was criticised for downplaying comic material), while others emphasise farce and revelry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the production's tone early: whether to prioritise comedy, satire, or to lean into more serious social readings. Example: a version that minimizes comic elements risks criticism for losing the play's comic identity; conversely, a purely farcical approach may minimize thematic depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of music and preservation/adaptation of songs
rubrics_metrics.description: Shakespeare tackled providing Twelfth Night with effective musical interludes; songs such as 'O Mistress Mine' and 'Come Away, Come Away, Death' have been widely set to music and musical adaptations and jukebox musicals exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to include original songs, new musical arrangements, or to create a full musical adaptation (examples: Your Own Thing, Play On!, Illyria). Consider composers and arrangements that support the play's mood; omitting music may lose an essential Elizabethan entertainment element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting and period choices that support theme
rubrics_metrics.description: Illyria is important to the play's romantic atmosphere; productions have set the play in varied contexts (19th century, circus world, 1980s Benidorm, contemporary Miami-inspired setting, Cuban refugee framing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a setting (period or modern location) that coherently supports the production's thematic priorities—romantic exoticism, carnival inversion, migration/identity, or comic social satire. Examples: preserving Illyria sustains historical/romantic tone; contemporary relocations can foreground migration, identity, or cultural specificity (e.g., 2023 St. Louis production emphasised migration and Latiné identity). Ensure setting changes are integrated into costume, music, and characterization to avoid dissonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve core plot mechanics: disguise, twins, mistaken identity
rubrics_metrics.description: The play centres on the twins Viola and Sebastian, mistaken identity, and Viola's cross-dressing as Cesario—these are central to the love-triangle and comedic confusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain the structural devices (shipwreck, twins, disguise, mistaken identity) or provide clear, well-motivated substitutions when adapting (modern analogues for shipwreck/arrival, believable mechanics for mistaken identity). Anti-pattern: altering or omitting the central identity-confusion without adequate replacement can undermine the plot's causal logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foregrounding gender and sexual identity themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Twelfth Night explores gender identity, cross-dressing, and sexual attraction; modern readings often treat androgyny and sexual ambiguity with immediacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide how explicitly to stage issues of same-sex attraction, androgyny, and gender performance. Productions can highlight these aspects (e.g., Royal Shakespeare Company’s 1966 production showing more physical attraction) or play them more subtly. Consider casting and direction choices that make gender dynamics legible to contemporary audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit metatheatrical elements and theatrical self-consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The play contains references to theatricality ('Are you a comedian?', 'I am not that I play'), the plot against Malvolio comments on theatricality, and Feste’s play-acting ('the old Vice' of Morality plays).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use staging and performance to draw attention to 'play-acting' and theatrical roles (doubling, actors commenting on performance). Emphasising metatheatre can enrich themes of disguise and role-play; ignoring it may flatten opportunities for theatrical commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation medium considerations (stage, film, television, radio, musical)
rubrics_metrics.description: Twelfth Night has been adapted to film, television, radio, opera, and musicals; each medium has its conventions and prior successful/unsuccessful approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor choices to medium-specific needs: film can alter scale and realism (but beware of stripping comedic elements, as critics noted), radio emphasizes vocal performance and music, musicals can foreground song-based storytelling, and opera/mixed-voice settings reinterpret the songs. Study precedents (e.g., 1996 Trevor Nunn film, 2006 She's the Man modernisation, multiple radio adaptations) to learn what choices worked or were criticised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Localise or translate Elizabethan references with care
rubrics_metrics.description: The play contains English allusions (e.g., 'Westward ho!', 'The Elephant' pub) and Elizabethan cultural markers that may be unfamiliar to modern audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to retain Elizabethan references (for authenticity) or translate/localise them for accessibility. If localising, provide equivalents that preserve humour or context; avoid leaving obscure references that hinder comprehension without explanatory staging or adaptation choices.
